I am seventy years old, and I have worked this land in Quzhou since I was twenty. My bones ache in the morning, but I still know every mu of my 8 mu field better than anyone. This year, I will plant all 8 mu to cotton, just as I have done for decades. My husband and I are the only ones left in the house, and our backs are not strong enough to manage more than one crop. Cotton is what this soil knows, and it is what I know.

I will buy the improved cotton seeds from the old supply shop in town—the same kind I have sown for many years. I do not bother with the new hybrid seeds the young people talk about. They cost too much money, and if they fail, I have no one to blame but myself. My seeds have never betrayed me.

When the earth warms in early spring, I will run the rotary tiller over the field to break up the soil. Deep ploughing is too hard for me now, and the rotary machine does a fine enough job. Before sowing, I will spread my base fertilizer—compound fertilizer I carry on my shoulder pole. Then, when the cotton flowers in summer, I will top-dress with urea. Altogether, I will put down about 15 kg of nitrogen per mu, with some phosphorus and potassium mixed in. I do not use more than that because over-fertilizing makes the plants tall and leafy but gives empty bolls, and fertilizer is expensive.

I have my well, and I will irrigate three times: once when I sow if the spring is dry, once when the flowers open, and once when the bolls are fattening. Water costs electricity, and I am careful. Three times is enough if you time them right. I watch the sky every day; I know when the rains will come.

For pests, mainly the cotton bollworm, I will spray four times. I walk my field every morning at dawn, and I know the smell of trouble. I do not spray blindly—I wait until I see the worms, then I act. Four sprays should keep them away.

I expect to harvest about 260 kg of seed cotton per mu this year. Some years the land gives 300, some years less, but 260 is an honest expectation for an old woman and her husband working alone. We will pick it by hand in the autumn, as we always have.
